fullPassage: Patterns such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos, or requiring an account just to make a purchase all interfere with the user's control over their own experience. From a sustainability perspective, many of these patterns encourage overconsumption of data and attention. Infinite scroll keeps loading new content whether the user wants it or not, increasing data usage and device processing. Autoplay forces media to load and play even for people who may never watch it. These choices consume more energy on both the user's device and the servers delivering the content. Take the decision by a popular music streaming platform to replace static album artwork with short video loops by default. This change significantly increases data usage and battery consumption, while the option to disable it is buried deep in the settings. As a result, most users consume more resources unless they actively search for a way to opt out. It is important to acknowledge that web design always nudges behavior in some way. Showing consequences and highlighting options are all forms of influence. The ethical line is not whether nudging exists, but whether it is transparent, reversible, and aligned with the user's interests. In many cases, the most responsible approach is to make the lower-impact option the default, while keeping alternatives clearly available. Defaults are powerful, and when chosen carefully, they can reduce environmental impact without removing user agency.
title: Ethical Defaults in Web Design
